<question>
our player keeps playing when a notification sound or another app takes audio. we have audio focus listeners but they don't seem to fire on some devices. what should I look at in the focus change callback?
</question>
<tool_calls>
- search_kb {"k": 3, "query": "audio focus transient loss pause duck notification call"}
  result: {"results": [{"id": "audio-focus", "title": "Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)", "text": "# Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.
- Without Media3, request focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` (API 26+) and react to
  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}, {"id": "av-sync", "title": "Audio and video drift out of sync", "text": "# Audio and video drift out of sync

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.
- Variable-frame-rate recordings (common from phone cameras) can drift when a pipeline assumes
  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.
- When writing a custom renderer, use `AudioTrack.getTimestamp()` to map audio frames to
  real time instead of counting written bytes."}, {"id": "behind-live-window", "title": "BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams", "text": "# BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams

A live stream exposes a sliding window of segments. If playback falls further behind than
the window (long pause, slow network, app in the background), the segments it needs are gone
and the player raises a `BehindLiveWindowExcep…
</tool_calls>
<answer>
Likely cause: The knowledge base only says that an app keeps playing over other audio when it never requests focus or ignores focus loss. It doesn't explain why listeners fail to fire on some devices, so I can't name a cause for that without seeing your code or logs. One possibility is that focus isn't actually being requested, or the listener isn't registered, on those devices.
Next step: Add logging at the top of your focus-change callback to see whether it fires at all on an affected device. If it never fires, check that the focus request was made and granted and that the listener is attached to it (`AudioFocusRequest` is API 26+). If it fires, check that you handle `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT` and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`. With Media3, `handleAudioFocus = true` in `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)` removes the need for your own callback.
Sources: [kb:audio-focus]
</answer>

messages.content:
<question>
How do I get our player to output HDR10 on lumen-l3? Right now the frames look tone-mapped to SDR on that device. Which Surface and color-space configuration do I need on lumen-l3 for the HDR path, and how do I confirm the display mode is actually switched?
</question>
<tool_calls>
- codec_caps {"device": "lumen-l3", "mime": "video/hevc"}
  result: {"android_api_level": 33, "decoders": [{"hardware": true, "max_fps_at_max_size": 60, "max_height": 1080, "max_width": 1920, "mime": "video/hevc", "name": "c2.lumen.hevc.decoder", "profiles": ["Main"]}], "device": "lumen-l3", "display_hdr_types": [], "max_concurrent_hw_video_decoders": 4, "mime": "video/hevc", "widevine_security_level": "L3"}
- search_kb {"k": 3, "query": "HDR10 output surface color space display mode"}
  result: {"results": [{"id": "hdr-tone-mapping", "title": "HDR video looks washed out or too dark", "text": "# HDR video looks washed out or too dark

HDR10 and HLG streams carry a wide colour gamut (BT.2020) and a high-dynamic-range transfer
function (PQ or HLG). When such a stream reaches a display path that is not HDR-capable and
nothing tone-maps it, colours look flat and grey or the picture looks far too dark.

Checks:
- Ask the display what it supports: `Display.getHdrCapabilities()` (or `Display.isHdr()` on API 26+).
- Render to a `SurfaceView`. `TextureView` composites through the GPU and is a common reason
  HDR output gets flattened.
- Confirm the decoder output format reports the expected colour transfer
  (`MediaFormat.KEY_COLOR_TRANSFER`) and colour standard.
- If the display is SDR, tone-map explicitly (for example with a Media3 Transformer or
  effect pipeline) or serve an SDR rendition."}, {"id": "mediacodec-errors", "title": "MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures", "text": "# MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures

`MediaCodec.CodecException` reports whether an error is transient (`isTransient()`: retry the
same call later) or recoverable (`isRecoverable()`: call `stop()`, `configure()`, `start()`
again). Anything else means releasing the codec and creating a new one.

Common causes:
- The format, profile, or level is not supported by any decoder on the device. Query
  `MediaCodecList` and `MediaCodecInfo.CodecCapabilities` before configuring.
- Too many codec instances are alive at once. Hardware codecs are a shared, limited resource;
  release codecs you no longer use.
- The output `Surface` was released while the codec still used it.

Log the `diagnosticInfo` string from the exception; it names the failing component."}]}
</tool_calls>
<answer>
Likely cause: No Surface or colour-space configuration will fix this on lumen-l3, because the device profile reports no HDR display types (display_hdr_types is empty) and its only HEVC decoder (c2.lumen.hevc.decoder) lists the Main profile only, up to 1920x1080, with no Main10, which HDR10 needs. The device is Android 33, but the display is SDR, so the SDR-looking output is expected, as the knowledge base describes for a non-HDR display with nothing tone-mapping.
Next step: Don't try to force an HDR10 path on lumen-l3. Serve an SDR rendition (or tone-map explicitly, for example with a Media3 Transformer or effect pipeline) for that device, and confirm on the device with Display.getHdrCapabilities()/Display.isHdr(), which should report no HDR types. Use a SurfaceView and check MediaFormat.KEY_COLOR_TRANSFER on an HDR-capable device instead.
Sources: [tool:codec_caps] [kb:hdr-tone-mapping]
</answer>

<question>
is hdr10_hevc_1080p.mp4 supposed to look HDR on lumen-l3 in our player? on the lumen-l3 it looks kinda washed out compared to the photos app. can you check if thats expected
</question>

  result: {"bit_rate": 833216, "duration_s": 1.0, "file": "hdr10_hevc_1080p.mp4", "format": "mov,mp4,m4a,3gp,3g2,mj2", "mp4_top_level_boxes": ["ftyp", "free", "mdat", "moov"], "streams": [{"avg_frame_rate": "24/1", "codec_name": "hevc", "codec_type": "video", "color_primaries": "bt2020", "color_space": "bt2020nc", "color_transfer": "smpte2084", "height": 1080, "index": 0, "pix_fmt": "yuv420p10le", "profile": "Main 10", "start_time": "0.000000", "width": 1920}]}
- codec_caps {"device": "lumen-l3", "mime": "video/hevc"}
  result: {"android_api_level": 33, "decoders": [{"hardware": true, "max_fps_at_max_size": 60, "max_height": 1080, "max_width": 1920, "mime": "video/hevc", "name": "c2.lumen.hevc.decoder", "profiles": ["Main"]}], "device": "lumen-l3", "display_hdr_types": [], "max_concurrent_hw_video_decoders": 4, "mime": "video/hevc", "widevine_security_level": "L3"}
</tool_calls>
<answer>
Likely cause: Yes, washed out is expected here. The file is HDR10 (hevc Main 10, bt2020, smpte2084 PQ transfer), but lumen-l3 reports no display HDR types and its hardware HEVC decoder lists only the Main profile, so there is no HDR display path and nothing tone-maps the PQ signal, which makes colours look flat and grey [kb:hdr-tone-mapping]. It is not supposed to look HDR on this device; the photos app probably tone-maps or handles it differently.
Next step: Tone-map explicitly in your player for devices with no HDR display (for example with a Media3 Transformer or effect pipeline), or serve an SDR rendition to lumen-l3. Also note the decoder doesn't list Main 10, so check the device can decode this 10-bit stream at all.

</answer>

<question>
lumen-l3 is failing on our higher-bitrate HEVC clips in the app. Can you help me work out which codec limits are being hit, and how to confirm it on the device?
</question>
<tool_calls>
- codec_caps {"device": "lumen-l3", "mime": "video/hevc"}
  result: {"android_api_level": 33, "decoders": [{"hardware": true, "max_fps_at_max_size": 60, "max_height": 1080, "max_width": 1920, "mime": "video/hevc", "name": "c2.lumen.hevc.decoder", "profiles": ["Main"]}], "device": "lumen-l3", "display_hdr_types": [], "max_concurrent_hw_video_decoders": 4, "mime": "video/hevc", "widevine_security_level": "L3"}
- search_kb {"k": 2, "query": "HEVC high bitrate codec level limits"}
  result: {"results": [{"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

Checks:
- Enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for the MIME type `video/av01`.
- On API 29+, `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` tells you whether a decoder is
  hardware backed.
- Use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check supported sizes and frame rates
  before choosing an AV1 rendition; fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC when needed."}, {"id": "mediacodec-errors", "title": "MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures", "text": "# MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures

`MediaCodec.CodecException` reports whether an error is transient (`isTransient()`: retry the
same call later) or recoverable (`isRecoverable()`: call `stop()`, `configure()`, `start()`
again). Anything else means releasing the codec and creating a new one.

Common causes:
- The format, profile, or level is not supported by any decoder on the device. Query
  `MediaCodecList` and `MediaCodecInfo.CodecCapabilities` before configuring.
- Too many codec instances are alive at once. Hardware codecs are a shared, limited resource;
  release codecs you no longer use.
- The output `Surface` was released while the codec still used it.

Log the `diagnosticInfo` string from the exception; it names the failing component."}]}
</tool_calls>
<answer>
Likely cause: codec_caps shows lumen-l3 has one hardware HEVC decoder (c2.lumen.hevc.decoder) limited to the Main profile, 1920x1080 at 60 fps, and no more than 4 concurrent hardware decoders. A high-bitrate clip that is above 1080p, above 60 fps, Main 10, or competing with other live decoders would exceed those limits. The tools give no bitrate or level limit for this decoder, so I cannot yet say the bitrate itself is the problem; the knowledge base only says an unsupported format, profile, or level is a common cause of configure failures.
Next step: Run ffprobe on a failing clip and compare its profile, resolution and frame rate against 1080p60 Main, then on the device read c2.lumen.hevc.decoder's CodecCapabilities (profileLevels and getVideoCapabilities().getBitrateRange() / isSizeSupported / areSizeAndRateSupported) for the exact level and bitrate ceiling, and log the exception's diagnosticInfo.
Sources: [tool:codec_caps] [kb:mediacodec-errors]
</answer>

</answer>

<question>
drm content only plays at low res on our cheap test phone, the nicer one is fine. is that expected or did we break something? how do i check what max resolution the drm license allows on that phone
</question>
<tool_calls>
- search_kb {"k": 2, "query": "DRM max resolution low-end phone Widevine L3 license policy"}
  result: {"results": [{"id": "widevine-levels", "title": "Widevine security levels and HD playback", "text": "# Widevine security levels and HD playback

Widevine has security levels: L1 (decryption and decoding inside a hardware trusted
environment) and L3 (software only). Content owners commonly restrict HD and higher
renditions to L1, so the same app may get only SD on an L3 device.

Checks:
- Read `MediaDrm(WIDEVINE_UUID).getPropertyString("securityLevel")`.
- A device can drop from L1 to L3 after an unlocked bootloader or a failed keybox
  provisioning; the license server then refuses HD keys.
- Log the license request and response status to tell a policy refusal apart from a
  network or provisioning error."}, {"id": "mp4-faststart", "title": "Progressive MP4 takes long to start (moov atom at the end)", "text": "# Progressive MP4 takes long to start (moov atom at the end)

An MP4 file's index (the `moov` atom) is often written at the end of the file by recorders and
encoders. A progressive-download player must then fetch the end of the file before playback can
begin, which shows up as a long start delay or extra range requests.

Checks and fix:
- `ffprobe -v trace file.mp4 2>&1 | grep -m2 -E "type:'(moov|mdat)'"` shows which atom comes first.
- Remux with the index at the front: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c copy -movflags +faststart out.mp4`.
- For adaptive streaming, prefer fragmented MP4 (DASH or HLS) instead."}]}
</tool_calls>
<answer>
Likely cause: This may well be expected: the knowledge base says Widevine L3 (software only) devices commonly get only SD, since content owners restrict HD and higher to L1, and a cheap phone is plausibly L3. I haven't confirmed the phone's actual level, because I don't have its device id, so I can't rule out that something broke, for example a device that dropped from L1 to L3 after an unlocked bootloader or failed keybox provisioning. The knowledge base doesn't describe a direct way to read the maximum resolution a license allows.
Next step: On the cheap phone, read `MediaDrm(WIDEVINE_UUID).getPropertyString("securityLevel")` and compare it with the nicer one. Then log the license request and response status on both to tell a policy refusal apart from a provisioning or network error. Send me the device id and I can look up its reported security level.
Sources: [kb:widevine-levels]
</answer>

<question>
How do I check or cap the DRM output resolution on lumen-l3? Our licensed content only comes out at SD on that device and I need to find where the limit is set.
</question>
<tool_calls>
- codec_caps {"device": "lumen-l3", "mime": "video/avc"}
  result: {"android_api_level": 33, "decoders": [{"hardware": true, "max_fps_at_max_size": 60, "max_height": 1080, "max_width": 1920, "mime": "video/avc", "name": "c2.lumen.avc.decoder", "profiles": ["Baseline", "Main", "High"]}], "device": "lumen-l3", "display_hdr_types": [], "max_concurrent_hw_video_decoders": 4, "mime": "video/avc", "widevine_security_level": "L3"}
- search_kb {"k": 3, "query": "Widevine security level L1 L3 resolution cap HD"}
  result: {"results": [{"id": "widevine-levels", "title": "Widevine security levels and HD playback", "text": "# Widevine security levels and HD playback

Widevine has security levels: L1 (decryption and decoding inside a hardware trusted
environment) and L3 (software only). Content owners commonly restrict HD and higher
renditions to L1, so the same app may get only SD on an L3 device.

Checks:
- Read `MediaDrm(WIDEVINE_UUID).getPropertyString("securityLevel")`.
- A device can drop from L1 to L3 after an unlocked bootloader or a failed keybox
  provisioning; the license server then refuses HD keys.
- Log the license request and response status to tell a policy refusal apart from a
  network or provisioning error."}, {"id": "mediacodec-errors", "title": "MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures", "text": "# MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures

`MediaCodec.CodecException` reports whether an error is transient (`isTransient()`: retry the
same call later) or recoverable (`isRecoverable()`: call `stop()`, `configure()`, `start()`
again). Anything else means releasing the codec and creating a new one.

Common causes:
- The format, profile, or level is not supported by any decoder on the device. Query
  `MediaCodecList` and `MediaCodecInfo.CodecCapabilities` before configuring.
- Too many codec instances are alive at once. Hardware codecs are a shared, limited resource;
  release codecs you no longer use.
- The output `Surface` was released while the codec still used it.

Log the `diagnosticInfo` string from the exception; it names the failing component."}]}
</tool_calls>
<answer>
Likely cause: There is no client-side resolution cap to find. codec_caps shows lumen-l3 reports Widevine security level L3 (software-only), and the KB says content owners commonly restrict HD and higher renditions to L1, so the license server hands out SD-only keys to an L3 device. The decoder itself is not the limit (the hardware AVC decoder supports up to 1920x1080 at 60 fps).
Next step: Confirm on the device with MediaDrm(WIDEVINE_UUID).getPropertyString("securityLevel") and log the license request/response status to see whether the server is refusing HD keys by policy; if it should be L1, check for an unlocked bootloader or failed keybox provisioning. Any cap lives in the license policy / content owner rules, not in a setting you can raise in the app.
Sources: [tool:codec_caps] [kb:widevine-levels]
</answer>

messages.content:
<question>
We target minSdk 21 and since AudioFocusRequest works from API 21 we can drop the legacy requestAudioFocus() path entirely. What is the cleanest way to build the AudioFocusRequest and handle onAudioFocusChange on API 21 through 25?
</question>
<tool_calls>
- search_kb {"k": 2, "query": "AudioFocusRequest API level minimum requestAudioFocus legacy"}
  result: {"results": [{"id": "audio-focus", "title": "Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)", "text": "# Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.
- Without Media3, request focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` (API 26+) and react to
  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}, {"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

Checks:
- Enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for the MIME type `video/av01`.
- On API 29+, `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` tells you whether a decoder is
  hardware backed.
- Use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check supported sizes and frame rates
  before choosing an AV1 rendition; fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC when needed."}]}
</tool_calls>
<answer>
Likely cause: That premise is wrong: the knowledge base says `AudioFocusRequest` is for API 26+, not API 21, so you can't drop the legacy path for API 21 through 25.
Next step: Branch by API level: use `AudioFocusRequest` on API 26+, and on API 21 to 25 use the legacy `AudioManager.requestAudioFocus(listener, streamType, durationHint)` overload (from my general knowledge, not the knowledge base, so check the docs). Share one `OnAudioFocusChangeListener` handling `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT` and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`. Or use Media3's `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)` with `handleAudioFocus = true`, which covers this for you.
Sources: [kb:audio-focus]
</answer>

A progressive-download player must then fetch the end of the file before playback can\nbegin, which shows up as a long start delay or extra range requests.\n\nChecks and fix:\n- `ffprobe -v trace file.mp4 2>&1 | grep -m2 -E \"type:'(moov|mdat)'\"` shows which atom comes first.\n- Remux with the index at the front: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c copy -movflags +faststart out.mp4`.\n- For adaptive streaming, prefer fragmented MP4 (DASH or HLS) instead."}]}

Likely cause: The premise does not hold: ffprobe lists the top-level boxes of progressive_faststart.mp4 as ftyp, moov, free, mdat, so the moov atom is already before mdat and the file is already faststart-laid-out. The stalled first byte-range request is therefore probably coming from somewhere else (for example the server, CDN or upload step not honouring range requests, or a different file than the one probed being uploaded).
Next step: Check the file that is actually being served, not just the export: run `ffprobe -v trace file.mp4 2>&1 | grep -m2 -E "type:'(moov|mdat)'"` on the uploaded copy, and if moov ever does come last, remux with `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c copy -movflags +faststart out.mp4` as the final pipeline step before upload. I found nothing in the tools or KB about a MediaExtractor check for moov position, so I would not rely on one; the ffprobe box-order check is the verified method.

</answer>

error code `ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW`.

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow

function (PQ or HLG). When such a stream reaches a display path that is not HDR-capable and

  HDR output gets flattened.

Widevine has security levels: L1 (decryption and decoding inside a hardware trusted
environment) and L3 (software only). Content owners commonly restrict HD and higher
renditions to L1, so the same app may get only SD on an L3 device.

Checks:
- Read `MediaDrm(WIDEVINE_UUID).getPropertyString("securityLevel")`.
- A device can drop from L1 to L3 after an unlocked bootloader or a failed keybox
  provisioning; the license server then refuses HD keys.
- Log the license request and response status to tell a policy refusal apart from a
  network or provisioning error."}, {"id": "behind-live-window", "title": "BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams", "text": "# BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams

A live stream exposes a sliding window of segments. If playback falls further behind than
the window (long pause, slow network, app in the background), the segments it needs are gone
and the player raises a `BehindLiveWindowException`, surfaced as a `PlaybackException` with
error code `ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW`.

Fix: in `Player.Listener.onPlayerError`, check for that error code, then call
`player.seekToDefaultPosition()` followed by `player.prepare()` to rejoin at the live edge.
Consider a longer live window on the server or a smaller target live offset on the client."}]}
</tool_calls>

(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

`MediaCodec.CodecException` reports whether an error is transient (`isTransient()`: retry the
same call later) or recoverable (`isRecoverable()`: call `stop()`, `configure()`, `start()`
again). Anything else means releasing the codec and creating a new one.

Common causes:
- The format, profile, or level is not supported by any decoder on the device. Query
  `MediaCodecList` and `MediaCodecInfo.CodecCapabilities` before configuring.
- Too many codec instances are alive at once. Hardware codecs are a shared, limited resource;
  release codecs you no longer use.
- The output `Surface` was released while the codec still used it.

Log the `diagnosticInfo` string from the exception; it names the failing component."}, {"id": "widevine-levels", "title": "Widevine security levels and HD playback", "text": "# Widevine security levels and HD playback

I haven't run any tools on your test device, so I can't tell which case it is.

<question>
Our live HLS player fails with BehindLiveWindowException (ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW, 1002) after the app returns from background. Should we recover by re-preparing the MediaItem, seeking to the default live position, or raising the live target offset? </question>
<tool_calls>
- search_kb {"k": 3, "query": "BehindLiveWindowException live window resume seekToDefaultPosition"}
  result: {"results": [{"id": "behind-live-window", "title": "BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams", "text": "# BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams\n\nA live stream exposes a sliding window of segments. If playback falls further behind than\nthe window (long pause, slow network, app in the background), the segments it needs are gone\nand the player raises a `BehindLiveWindowException`, surfaced as a `PlaybackException` with\nerror code `ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW`.\n\nFix: in `Player.Listener.onPlayerError`, check for that error code, then call\n`player.seekToDefaultPosition()` followed by `player.prepare()` to rejoin at the live edge.\nConsider a longer live window on the server or a smaller target live offset on the client."}]}
</tool_calls>
<answer>
Likely cause: While the app is in the background the player falls further behind than the live stream's sliding window, so the segments it needs are gone and it raises BehindLiveWindowException (ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW) [kb:behind-live-window].
Next step: Use the documented fix, and put it in Player.Listener.onPlayerError rather than the lifecycle callback: when the error code is ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW, call player.seekToDefaultPosition() and then player.prepare() to rejoin at the live edge. That is a seek to the default live position followed by a re-prepare, not a new MediaItem. Raising the live target offset is not the fix; the note only suggests optionally a longer live window on the server or a smaller target live offset on the client to make it less likely. The knowledge base doesn't say anything about handling it in a lifecycle callback.
Sources: [kb:behind-live-window]
</answer>

<question>
drm content only plays at low res on our cheap test phone, the nicer one is fine. is that expected or did we break something? how do i check what max resolution the drm license allows on that phone
</question>
<tool_calls>
- search_kb {"k": 2, "query": "DRM max resolution low-end phone Widevine L3 license policy"}
  result: {"results": [{"id": "widevine-levels", "title": "Widevine security levels and HD playback", "text": "# Widevine security levels and HD playback

Widevine has security levels: L1 (decryption and decoding inside a hardware trusted
environment) and L3 (software only). Content owners commonly restrict HD and higher
renditions to L1, so the same app may get only SD on an L3 device.

Checks:
- Read `MediaDrm(WIDEVINE_UUID).getPropertyString("securityLevel")`.
- A device can drop from L1 to L3 after an unlocked bootloader or a failed keybox
  provisioning; the license server then refuses HD keys.
- Log the license request and response status to tell a policy refusal apart from a
  network or provisioning error."}, {"id": "mp4-faststart", "title": "Progressive MP4 takes long to start (moov atom at the end)", "text": "# Progressive MP4 takes long to start (moov atom at the end)

An MP4 file's index (the `moov` atom) is often written at the end of the file by recorders and
encoders. A progressive-download player must then fetch the end of the file before playback can
begin, which shows up as a long start delay or extra range requests.

Checks and fix:
- `ffprobe -v trace file.mp4 2>&1 | grep -m2 -E "type:'(moov|mdat)'"` shows which atom comes first.
- Remux with the index at the front: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c copy -movflags +faststart out.mp4`.
- For adaptive streaming, prefer fragmented MP4 (DASH or HLS) instead."}]}
</tool_calls>
<answer>
Likely cause: This may well be expected: the knowledge base says Widevine L3 (software only) devices commonly get only SD, since content owners restrict HD and higher to L1, and a cheap phone is plausibly L3. I haven't confirmed the phone's actual level, because I don't have its device id, so I can't rule out that something broke, for example a device that dropped from L1 to L3 after an unlocked bootloader or failed keybox provisioning. The knowledge base doesn't describe a direct way to read the maximum resolution a license allows.
Next step: On the cheap phone, read `MediaDrm(WIDEVINE_UUID).getPropertyString("securityLevel")` and compare it with the nicer one. Then log the license request and response status on both to tell a policy refusal apart from a provisioning or network error. Send me the device id and I can look up its reported security level.
Sources: [kb:widevine-levels]
</answer>

- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}, {"id": "av-sync", "title": "Audio and video drift out of sync", "text": "# Audio and video drift out of sync

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.

  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.

  real time instead of counting written bytes."}, {"id": "behind-live-window", "title": "BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams", "text": "# BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams

A live stream exposes a sliding window of segments. If playback falls further behind than
the window (long pause, slow network, app in the background), the segments it needs are gone
and the player raises a `BehindLiveWindowExcep…
</tool_calls>

Likely cause: The knowledge base only says that an app keeps playing over other audio when it never requests focus or ignores focus loss. It doesn't explain why listeners fail to fire on some devices, so I can't name a cause for that without seeing your code or logs. One possibility is that focus isn't actually being requested, or the listener isn't registered, on those devices.
Next step: Add logging at the top of your focus-change callback to see whether it fires at all on an affected device. With Media3, `handleAudioFocus = true` in `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)` removes the need for your own callback.

</answer>

android has had av1 decoding since android 8 so our av1 streams should play on everything above that, right? how do i set that up in the player so it picks av1 when the phone supports it
</question>
<tool_calls>
- search_kb {"k": 2, "query": "AV1 decoder Android version support hardware software fallback"}
  result: {"results": [{"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

Checks:
- Enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for the MIME type `video/av01`.
- On API 29+, `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` tells you whether a decoder is
  hardware backed.
- Use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check supported sizes and frame rates
  before choosing an AV1 rendition; fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC when needed."}, {"id": "mediacodec-errors", "title": "MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures", "text": "# MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures

`MediaCodec.CodecException` reports whether an error is transient (`isTransient()`: retry the
same call later) or recoverable (`isRecoverable()`: call `stop()`, `configure()`, `start()`
again). Anything else means releasing the codec and creating a new one.

Common causes:
- The format, profile, or level is not supported by any decoder on the device. Query
  `MediaCodecList` and `MediaCodecInfo.CodecCapabilities` before configuring.
- Too many codec instances are alive at once. Hardware codecs are a shared, limited resource;
  release codecs you no longer use.
- The output `Surface` was released while the codec still used it.

Log the `diagnosticInfo` string from the exception; it names the failing component."}]}
</tool_calls>
<answer>
Likely cause: That isn't right: Android's software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) ships from Android 10 (API 29), not Android 8, and hardware AV1 depends on the SoC rather than the Android version. Many devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 only in software, which can be too slow at high resolutions or frame rates. So AV1 won't play well on everything above Android 8.
Next step: Make the player choose at runtime: enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for `video/av01`, check `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` (API 29+), and use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check sizes and frame rates against your AV1 rendition. Select AV1 only when a suitable decoder passes, and otherwise fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC.
Sources: [kb:av1-decoding]
</answer>

messages.content:
<question>
Since Android has shipped an AV1 decoder since Android 8, we can drop the software fallback for AV1 on our build. How should we check the codec list at runtime to choose between the hardware AV1 decoder and the software one, and is there a reason to keep a fallback?
</question>
<answer>
Likely cause: The premise is wrong: Android's software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) ships from Android 10 (API 29), not Android 8, and hardware AV1 depends on the SoC, not the Android version. Many devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 only in software, which can be too slow at high resolutions or frame rates. So there is a good reason to keep the fallback logic.
Next step: At runtime, enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for `video/av01`, use `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` (API 29+) to tell the hardware decoder from the software one, and check `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` for the sizes and frame rates you plan to serve. Prefer a hardware decoder if it qualifies, accept the software one only if it can keep up, and otherwise fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC.
Sources: [kb:av1-decoding]
</answer>

messages.content:
<question>
On the HDR path we pass HDR10 static metadata through MediaFormat KEY_HDR_STATIC_INFO, but the decoder output still looks flat on the panel. Which of the colour transfer and mastering display fields should we check first to find where the metadata gets dropped?
</question>
<tool_calls>
- search_kb {"k": 2, "query": "HDR10 static metadata KEY_HDR_STATIC_INFO colour transfer mastering display"}
  result: {"results": [{"id": "hdr-tone-mapping", "title": "HDR video looks washed out or too dark", "text": "# HDR video looks washed out or too dark

HDR10 and HLG streams carry a wide colour gamut (BT.2020) and a high-dynamic-range transfer
function (PQ or HLG). When such a stream reaches a display path that is not HDR-capable and
nothing tone-maps it, colours look flat and grey or the picture looks far too dark.

Checks:
- Ask the display what it supports: `Display.getHdrCapabilities()` (or `Display.isHdr()` on API 26+).
- Render to a `SurfaceView`. `TextureView` composites through the GPU and is a common reason
  HDR output gets flattened.
- Confirm the decoder output format reports the expected colour transfer
  (`MediaFormat.KEY_COLOR_TRANSFER`) and colour standard.
- If the display is SDR, tone-map explicitly (for example with a Media3 Transformer or
  effect pipeline) or serve an SDR rendition."}]}
</tool_calls>
<answer>
Likely cause: Flat output on an HDR panel usually means the HDR signalling was lost or never reached a display path that can show it. The knowledge base doesn't cover KEY_HDR_STATIC_INFO or the individual mastering-display fields, so I can't tell you which of those is dropped; what it does say to check is the decoder output colour transfer and colour standard, plus the surface and display capability.

<question>
Since Android has shipped an AV1 decoder since Android 8, we can drop the software fallback for AV1 on our build. How should we check the codec list at runtime to choose between the hardware AV1 decoder and the software one, and is there a reason to keep a fallback?
</question>
<tool_calls>
- search_kb {"k": 2, "query": "AV1 decoder Android version hardware software fallback MediaCodecList"}
  result: {"results": [{"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

Checks:
- Enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for the MIME type `video/av01`.
- On API 29+, `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` tells you whether a decoder is
  hardware backed.
- Use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check supported sizes and frame rates
  before choosing an AV1 rendition; fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC when needed."}, {"id": "mediacodec-errors", "title": "MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures", "text": "# MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures

`MediaCodec.CodecException` reports whether an error is transient (`isTransient()`: retry the
same call later) or recoverable (`isRecoverable()`: call `stop()`, `configure()`, `start()`
again). Anything else means releasing the codec and creating a new one.

Common causes:
- The format, profile, or level is not supported by any decoder on the device. Query
  `MediaCodecList` and `MediaCodecInfo.CodecCapabilities` before configuring.
- Too many codec instances are alive at once. Hardware codecs are a shared, limited resource;
  release codecs you no longer use.
- The output `Surface` was released while the codec still used it.

Log the `diagnosticInfo` string from the exception; it names the failing component."}]}
</tool_calls>
<answer>
Likely cause: The premise is wrong: Android's software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) ships from Android 10 (API 29), not Android 8, and hardware AV1 depends on the SoC, not the Android version. Many devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 only in software, which can be too slow at high resolutions or frame rates. So there is a good reason to keep the fallback logic.
Next step: At runtime, enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for `video/av01`, use `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` (API 29+) to tell the hardware decoder from the software one, and check `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` for the sizes and frame rates you plan to serve. Prefer a hardware decoder if it qualifies, accept the software one only if it can keep up, and otherwise fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC.
Sources: [kb:av1-decoding]
</answer>

<question>
hdr looks wrong on some phones, flat and grey. why would the same video look different per device, is it the file or the phone
</question>
<tool_calls>

  result: {"results": [{"id": "hdr-tone-mapping", "title": "HDR video looks washed out or too dark", "text": "# HDR video looks washed out or too dark

HDR10 and HLG streams carry a wide colour gamut (BT.2020) and a high-dynamic-range transfer
function (PQ or HLG). When such a stream reaches a display path that is not HDR-capable and
nothing tone-maps it, colours look flat and grey or the picture looks far too dark.

Checks:
- Ask the display what it supports: `Display.getHdrCapabilities()` (or `Display.isHdr()` on API 26+).
- Render to a `SurfaceView`. `TextureView` composites through the GPU and is a common reason
  HDR output gets flattened.
- Confirm the decoder output format reports the expected colour transfer
  (`MediaFormat.KEY_COLOR_TRANSFER`) and colour standard.
- If the display is SDR, tone-map explicitly (for example with a Media3 Transformer or
  effect pipeline) or serve an SDR rendition."}, {"id": "av-sync", "title": "Audio and video drift out of sync", "text": "# Audio and video drift out of sync

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.
- Variable-frame-rate recordings (common from phone cameras) can drift when a pipeline assumes
  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.
- When writing a custom renderer, use `AudioTrack.getTimestamp()` to map audio frames to
  real time instead of counting written bytes."}, {"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: ma…
</tool_calls>
<answer>
Likely cause: The same HDR file can look different per device because the result depends on the display and render path as well as the file. The knowledge base says HDR10/HLG streams look flat and grey when they reach a display path that is not HDR-capable and nothing tone-maps them, and that rendering through a TextureView (GPU compositing) is a common reason HDR gets flattened. I haven't inspected your file or any specific phone, so I can't say yet which applies here.
Next step: Compare a bad phone with a good one: check Display.getHdrCapabilities() / Display.isHdr() on each, and confirm the decoder output format reports the expected colour transfer (MediaFormat.KEY_COLOR_TRANSFER) and colour standard. If the bad phones report an SDR display, the phone is the limit, so tone-map or serve an SDR rendition; if they report HDR, check that you render to a SurfaceView rather than a TextureView.
Sources: [kb:hdr-tone-mapping]
</answer>

<question>
Our live HLS player fails with BehindLiveWindowException (ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW, 1002) after the app returns from background. Should we recover by re-preparing the MediaItem, seeking to the default live position, or raising the live target offset? Which of these is the supported fix, and where should the recovery live: onPlayerError or the lifecycle callback?
</question>
<answer>
Likely cause: While the app is in the background the player falls further behind than the live stream's sliding window, so the segments it needs are gone and it raises BehindLiveWindowException (ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW) [kb:behind-live-window].
Next step: Use the documented fix, and put it in Player.Listener.onPlayerError rather than the lifecycle callback: when the error code is ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW, call player.seekToDefaultPosition() and then player.prepare() to rejoin at the live edge. That is a seek to the default live position followed by a re-prepare, not a new MediaItem. Raising the live target offset is not the fix; the note only suggests optionally a longer live window on the server or a smaller target live offset on the client to make it less likely. The knowledge base doesn't say anything about handling it in a lifecycle callback.
Sources: [kb:behind-live-window]
</answer>

  result: {"results": [{"id": "audio-focus", "title": "Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)", "text": "# Audio keeps playing over calls or other apps (audio focus)

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.
- Without Media3, request focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` (API 26+) and react to
  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}, {"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

Checks:
- Enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for the MIME type `video/av01`.
- On API 29+, `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` tells you whether a decoder is
  hardware backed.
- Use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check supported sizes and frame rates
  before choosing an AV1 rendition; fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC when needed."}, {"id": "hdr-tone-mapping", "title": "HDR video looks washed out or too dark", "text": "# HDR video looks washed out or too dark

HDR10 and HLG streams carry a wide colour gamut (BT.2020) and a high-dynamic-range transfer
function (PQ or HLG). When such a stream reaches a display path that is not HDR-capable and
nothing tone-maps it, colours look flat and grey or the pic…
</tool_calls>
<answer>
Likely cause: No: the knowledge base says `AudioFocusRequest` is for API 26+, not API 21, so it won't work as a single approach on older devices.
Next step: The simplest setup is Media3: `player.setAudioAttributes(AudioAttributes.Builder().setUsage(C.USAGE_MEDIA).setContentType(C.AUDIO_CONTENT_TYPE_MUSIC).build(), true)`, where `true` is `handleAudioFocus`, so the player requests focus and pauses or ducks for you (the exact snippet is from my general knowledge, so check it against the Media3 docs). If you manage focus yourself, use `AudioFocusRequest` on API 26+ and the legacy `AudioManager.requestAudioFocus(listener, streamType, durationHint)` on older versions, and react in your listener to `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT` and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
Sources: [kb:audio-focus]
</answer>

<question>
our player keeps playing when a notification sound or another app takes audio. we have audio focus listeners but they don't seem to fire on some devices. what should I look at in the focus change callback?
</question>
<answer>
Likely cause: The knowledge base only says that an app keeps playing over other audio when it never requests focus or ignores focus loss. It doesn't explain why listeners fail to fire on some devices, so I can't name a cause for that without seeing your code or logs. One possibility is that focus isn't actually being requested, or the listener isn't registered, on those devices.
Next step: Add logging at the top of your focus-change callback to see whether it fires at all on an affected device. If it never fires, check that the focus request was made and granted and that the listener is attached to it (`AudioFocusRequest` is API 26+). If it fires, check that you handle `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT` and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`. With Media3, `handleAudioFocus = true` in `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)` removes the need for your own callback.
Sources: [kb:audio-focus]
</answer>

</answer>

messages.content:
<question>
Since Android has shipped an AV1 decoder since Android 8, we can drop the software fallback for AV1 on our build. How should we check the codec list at runtime to choose between the hardware AV1 decoder and the software one, and is there a reason to keep a fallback?
</question>
<tool_calls>
- search_kb {"k": 2, "query": "AV1 decoder Android version hardware software fallback MediaCodecList"}
  result: {"results": [{"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

Checks:
- Enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for the MIME type `video/av01`.
- On API 29+, `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` tells you whether a decoder is
  hardware backed.
- Use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check supported sizes and frame rates
  before choosing an AV1 rendition; fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC when needed."}, {"id": "mediacodec-errors", "title": "MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures", "text": "# MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures

`MediaCodec.CodecException` reports whether an error is transient (`isTransient()`: retry the
same call later) or recoverable (`isRecoverable()`: call `stop()`, `configure()`, `start()`
again). Anything else means releasing the codec and creating a new one.

Common causes:
- The format, profile, or level is not supported by any decoder on the device. Query
  `MediaCodecList` and `MediaCodecInfo.CodecCapabilities` before configuring.
- Too many codec instances are alive at once. Hardware codecs are a shared, limited resource;
  release codecs you no longer use.
- The output `Surface` was released while the codec still used it.

Log the `diagnosticInfo` string from the exception; it names the failing component."}]}
</tool_calls>
<answer>
Likely cause: The premise is wrong: Android's software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) ships from Android 10 (API 29), not Android 8, and hardware AV1 depends on the SoC, not the Android version. Many devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 only in software, which can be too slow at high resolutions or frame rates. So there is a good reason to keep the fallback logic.
Next step: At runtime, enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for `video/av01`, use `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` (API 29+) to tell the hardware decoder from the software one, and check `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` for the sizes and frame rates you plan to serve. Prefer a hardware decoder if it qualifies, accept the software one only if it can keep up, and otherwise fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC.
Sources: [kb:av1-decoding]
</answer>

<question>

  result: {"results": [{"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

Checks:
- Enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for the MIME type `video/av01`.
- On API 29+, `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` tells you whether a decoder is
  hardware backed.
- Use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check supported sizes and frame rates
  before choosing an AV1 rendition; fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC when needed."}, {"id": "mediacodec-errors", "title": "MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures", "text": "# MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures

`MediaCodec.CodecException` reports whether an error is transient (`isTransient()`: retry the
same call later) or recoverable (`isRecoverable()`: call `stop()`, `configure()`, `start()`
again). Anything else means releasing the codec and creating a new one.

Common causes:
- The format, profile, or level is not supported by any decoder on the device. Query
  `MediaCodecList` and `MediaCodecInfo.CodecCapabilities` before configuring.
- Too many codec instances are alive at once. Hardware codecs are a shared, limited resource;
  release codecs you no longer use.
- The output `Surface` was released while the codec still used it.

Log the `diagnosticInfo` string from the exception; it names the failing component."}]}
</tool_calls>
<answer>
Likely cause: That isn't right: Android's software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) ships from Android 10 (API 29), not Android 8, and hardware AV1 depends on the SoC rather than the Android version. Many devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 only in software, which can be too slow at high resolutions or frame rates. So AV1 won't play well on everything above Android 8.
Next step: Make the player choose at runtime: enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for `video/av01`, check `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` (API 29+), and use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check sizes and frame rates against your AV1 rendition. Select AV1 only when a suitable decoder passes, and otherwise fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC.

<question>

Likely cause: Washed-out grey HDR10 usually means the stream (BT.2020, PQ transfer) reaches a path that is not HDR-capable or gets flattened and nothing tone-maps it; a TextureView composites through the GPU and is a common reason HDR gets flattened [kb:hdr-tone-mapping]. Next step: On an affected phone, query Display.getHdrCapabilities() (or Display.isHdr()): if it reports no HDR, the display path is the issue and you should tone-map or serve an SDR rendition; if it reports HDR, check that the player renders to a SurfaceView rather than a TextureView and that the decoder output format shows the expected KEY_COLOR_TRANSFER. Since the system gallery looks fine on the same phone, the player's surface/output path is the more likely culprit when the display reports HDR.
Sources: [kb:hdr-tone-mapping]
</answer>

<question>
progressive_faststart.mp4 came out of our export with the moov atom at the end of the file, so the first byte-range request stalls on mobile. What is the cleanest way to re-run faststart in our pipeline, and is there a MediaExtractor check that confirms the moov position before we upload?
</question>
<answer>
Likely cause: The premise does not hold: ffprobe lists the top-level boxes of progressive_faststart.mp4 as ftyp, moov, free, mdat, so the moov atom is already before mdat and the file is already faststart-laid-out. The stalled first byte-range request is therefore probably coming from somewhere else (for example the server, CDN or upload step not honouring range requests, or a different file than the one probed being uploaded).
Next step: Check the file that is actually being served, not just the export: run `ffprobe -v trace file.mp4 2>&1 | grep -m2 -E "type:'(moov|mdat)'"` on the uploaded copy, and if moov ever does come last, remux with `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -c copy -movflags +faststart out.mp4` as the final pipeline step before upload. I found nothing in the tools or KB about a MediaExtractor check for moov position, so I would not rely on one; the ffprobe box-order check is the verified method.
Sources: [tool:ffprobe] [kb:mp4-faststart]
</answer>

<question>
How do I check or cap the DRM output resolution on lumen-l3? Our licensed content only comes out at SD on that device and I need to find where the limit is set.
</question>
<tool_calls>
- codec_caps {"device": "lumen-l3", "mime": "video/avc"}
  result: {"android_api_level": 33, "decoders": [{"hardware": true, "max_fps_at_max_size": 60, "max_height": 1080, "max_width": 1920, "mime": "video/avc", "name": "c2.lumen.avc.decoder", "profiles": ["Baseline", "Main", "High"]}], "device": "lumen-l3", "display_hdr_types": [], "max_concurrent_hw_video_decoders": 4, "mime": "video/avc", "widevine_security_level": "L3"}
- search_kb {"k": 3, "query": "Widevine security level L1 L3 resolution cap HD"}
  result: {"results": [{"id": "widevine-levels", "title": "Widevine security levels and HD playback", "text": "# Widevine security levels and HD playback

Widevine has security levels: L1 (decryption and decoding inside a hardware trusted
environment) and L3 (software only). Content owners commonly restrict HD and higher
renditions to L1, so the same app may get only SD on an L3 device.

Checks:
- Read `MediaDrm(WIDEVINE_UUID).getPropertyString("securityLevel")`.
- A device can drop from L1 to L3 after an unlocked bootloader or a failed keybox
  provisioning; the license server then refuses HD keys.
- Log the license request and response status to tell a policy refusal apart from a
  network or provisioning error."}, {"id": "mediacodec-errors", "title": "MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures", "text": "# MediaCodec.CodecException and configure failures

`MediaCodec.CodecException` reports whether an error is transient (`isTransient()`: retry the
same call later) or recoverable (`isRecoverable()`: call `stop()`, `configure()`, `start()`
again). Anything else means releasing the codec and creating a new one.

Common causes:
- The format, profile, or level is not supported by any decoder on the device. Query
  `MediaCodecList` and `MediaCodecInfo.CodecCapabilities` before configuring.
- Too many codec instances are alive at once. Hardware codecs are a shared, limited resource;
  release codecs you no longer use.
- The output `Surface` was released while the codec still used it.

Log the `diagnosticInfo` string from the exception; it names the failing component."}]}
</tool_calls>
<answer>
Likely cause: There is no client-side resolution cap to find. codec_caps shows lumen-l3 reports Widevine security level L3 (software-only), and the KB says content owners commonly restrict HD and higher renditions to L1, so the license server hands out SD-only keys to an L3 device. The decoder itself is not the limit (the hardware AVC decoder supports up to 1920x1080 at 60 fps).
Next step: Confirm on the device with MediaDrm(WIDEVINE_UUID).getPropertyString("securityLevel") and log the license request/response status to see whether the server is refusing HD keys by policy; if it should be L1, check for an unlocked bootloader or failed keybox provisioning. Any cap lives in the license policy / content owner rules, not in a setting you can raise in the app.
Sources: [tool:codec_caps] [kb:widevine-levels]
</answer>

Android coordinates audio between apps with audio focus. An app that never requests focus,
or ignores focus loss, keeps playing over navigation prompts, calls, or other media.

Fix:
- With Media3, pass suitable `AudioAttributes` and `handleAudioFocus = true` to
  `ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...)`; the player then requests focus, ducks, and pauses for you.
- Without Media3, request focus with an `AudioFocusRequest` (API 26+) and react to
  `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS`, `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT`, and `AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK`.
- Also handle `ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY` to pause when headphones are unplugged."}, {"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: many
devices on recent Android releases still decode AV1 in software only, which can be too slow
for high resolutions or frame rates.

Checks:
- Enumerate `MediaCodecList(MediaCodecList.REGULAR_CODECS)` for the MIME type `video/av01`.
- On API 29+, `MediaCodecInfo.isHardwareAccelerated()` tells you whether a decoder is
  hardware backed.
- Use `CodecCapabilities.getVideoCapabilities()` to check supported sizes and frame rates
  before choosing an AV1 rendition; fall back to VP9 or H.264/HEVC when needed."}]}
</tool_calls>
<answer>
Likely cause: The premise does not hold: the knowledge base says AudioFocusRequest is API 26+, not API 21, so a builder-based AudioFocusRequest path will not cover a matrix that goes down to API 21. For API 21 to 25 you need the older requestAudioFocus(listener, streamType, durationHint) call (my KB search did not cover that API, so this is general Android knowledge).
Next step: Easiest is to avoid hand-rolling it: with Media3, pass AudioAttributes (usage USAGE_MEDIA, content type matching your audio) and handleAudioFocus = true to ExoPlayer.setAudioAttributes(...), and the player requests focus, ducks and pauses on every API level for you. If you write it yourself, request AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN with USAGE_MEDIA, and handle AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS, AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT and AUDIOFOCUS_LOSS_TRANSIENT_CAN_DUCK (lower volume on can-duck, pause on the others), using AudioFocusRequest only on API 26+ and the legacy call below that. Also handle ACTION_AUDIO_BECOMING_NOISY.
Sources: [kb:audio-focus]
</answer>

<question>
HDR10 content looks washed out in our player on some phones but plays fine in the system gallery. we set the surface with default color settings. what should we check first to tell whether it's the player or the display path?
</question>
<tool_calls>
- search_kb {"k": 3, "query": "HDR flat grey washed out colour transfer display HDR support tone mapping default surface color"}
  result: {"results": [{"id": "hdr-tone-mapping", "title": "HDR video looks washed out or too dark", "text": "# HDR video looks washed out or too dark

HDR10 and HLG streams carry a wide colour gamut (BT.2020) and a high-dynamic-range transfer
function (PQ or HLG). When such a stream reaches a display path that is not HDR-capable and
nothing tone-maps it, colours look flat and grey or the picture looks far too dark.

Checks:
- Ask the display what it supports: `Display.getHdrCapabilities()` (or `Display.isHdr()` on API 26+).
- Render to a `SurfaceView`. `TextureView` composites through the GPU and is a common reason
  HDR output gets flattened.
- Confirm the decoder output format reports the expected colour transfer
  (`MediaFormat.KEY_COLOR_TRANSFER`) and colour standard.
- If the display is SDR, tone-map explicitly (for example with a Media3 Transformer or
  effect pipeline) or serve an SDR rendition."}, {"id": "av-sync", "title": "Audio and video drift out of sync", "text": "# Audio and video drift out of sync

Players normally treat the audio clock as the master and schedule video frames against it.
Drift usually comes from wrong timestamps rather than from rendering speed.

Checks:
- Inspect stream start times and timestamps with `ffprobe -show_streams -show_frames`; a large
  `start_time` difference between audio and video streams shows up as constant offset.
- Variable-frame-rate recordings (common from phone cameras) can drift when a pipeline assumes
  a constant frame rate. Remux or transcode with correct timestamps.
- When writing a custom renderer, use `AudioTrack.getTimestamp()` to map audio frames to
  real time instead of counting written bytes."}, {"id": "av1-decoding", "title": "AV1 decoding support on Android", "text": "# AV1 decoding support on Android

Android ships a software AV1 decoder (`c2.android.av1.decoder`) starting with Android 10
(API 29). Hardware AV1 decoding depends on the device's SoC, not on the Android version: ma…
</tool_calls>
<answer>
Likely cause: Washed-out grey HDR10 usually means the stream (BT.2020, PQ transfer) reaches a path that is not HDR-capable or gets flattened and nothing tone-maps it; a TextureView composites through the GPU and is a common reason HDR gets flattened [kb:hdr-tone-mapping]. I haven't tested any specific phone, so I can't say yet which of these applies to yours.
Next step: On an affected phone, query Display.getHdrCapabilities() (or Display.isHdr()): if it reports no HDR, the display path is the issue and you should tone-map or serve an SDR rendition; if it reports HDR, check that the player renders to a SurfaceView rather than a TextureView and that the decoder output format shows the expected KEY_COLOR_TRANSFER. Since the system gallery looks fine on the same phone, the player's surface/output path is the more likely culprit when the display reports HDR.
Sources: [kb:hdr-tone-mapping]
</answer>

<question>
Our live HLS player fails with BehindLiveWindowException (ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW, 1002) after the app returns from background. Should we recover by re-preparing the MediaItem, seeking to the default live position, or raising the live target offset? Which of these is the supported fix, and where should the recovery live: onPlayerError or the lifecycle callback?
</question>
<tool_calls>
- search_kb {"k": 3, "query": "BehindLiveWindowException live window resume seekToDefaultPosition"}
  result: {"results": [{"id": "behind-live-window", "title": "BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams", "text": "# BehindLiveWindowException in Media3 / ExoPlayer live streams\n\nA live stream exposes a sliding window of segments. If playback falls further behind than\nthe window (long pause, slow network, app in the background), the segments it needs are gone\nand the player raises a `BehindLiveWindowException`, surfaced as a `PlaybackException` with\nerror code `ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW`.\n\nFix: in `Player.Listener.onPlayerError`, check for that error code, then call\n`player.seekToDefaultPosition()` followed by `player.prepare()` to rejoin at the live edge.\nConsider a longer live window on the server or a smaller target live offset on the client."}]}
</tool_calls>
<answer>
Likely cause: While the app is in the background the player falls further behind than the live stream's sliding window, so the segments it needs are gone and it raises BehindLiveWindowException (ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW) [kb:behind-live-window].
Next step: Use the documented fix, and put it in Player.Listener.onPlayerError rather than the lifecycle callback: when the error code is ERROR_CODE_BEHIND_LIVE_WINDOW, call player.seekToDefaultPosition() and then player.prepare() to rejoin at the live edge. That is a seek to the default live position followed by a re-prepare, not a new MediaItem. Raising the live target offset is not the fix; the note only suggests optionally a longer live window on the server or a smaller target live offset on the client to make it less likely. The knowledge base doesn't say anything about handling it in a lifecycle callback.
Sources: [kb:behind-live-window]
</answer>
